Maladaptive Strategies.value: I work hard at keeping busy with other things
I think about how life would have been different if the event had not occurred
I avoid eating or restrict food as a way of coping

Threat.value: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day
I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds

Memory.value: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order
I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns

Negative Appraisals.value: I can't stop bad things from happening to me
I should have protected others and I failed
The event happened because of the way I acted

issues.explanation: Fire/flame cues are hard to reconcile with a childhood domestic-violence witnessing trauma profile when the rest of the trigger, memory, threat, and appraisal items do not suggest fire, arson, or burn-related trauma content. This trigger appears trauma-incongruent rather than merely unusual.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me
issues.explanation: 'No longer capable of doing the things that defined me' suggests a loss of prior adult identity/functioning that is difficult to fit with a 19-year-old whose index trauma was childhood witnessed domestic violence. The other appraisals center on helplessness and failed protection, which fit better; this item is comparatively implausible for the developmental context.

vignette:
Valentina Reyes is a nineteen-year-old Salvadoran American woman who works as a train conductor on a regional commuter line - a job she took, she has said, because the schedule kept her moving and the noise of the rails drowned out her own thoughts. She presented for treatment with a PCL-5 score of 64, describing a childhood shaped by repeated exposure to her father's violence against her mother, and a present life that has never fully separated itself from those years.

The events Valentina remembers most vividly unfolded in the family's apartment when she was between seven and eleven years old. The incidents followed a recognisable pattern: her father would return late, the front door would slam, and the shouting would begin in the dark hallway outside her bedroom. She would lie still, listening, her heart hammering against her ribs, until the sounds escalated into something she could no longer ignore. On the worst nights she would creep to her doorway and watch, frozen, as her mother was struck against the kitchen wall. She never intervened. She was a child, but she has never forgiven herself for that stillness, and the belief that she should have done something - that her failure to act was a choice rather than an impossibility - has calcified into something she carries as fact.

In the years since leaving that household, Valentina has found that certain moments collapse the distance between then and now with a violence of their own. When she is working a night shift and the cab goes dark between stations, the blackness feels indistinguishable from the hallway of her childhood apartment, and the memory returns not as recollection but as event - disordered, non-linear, arriving with the taste of something metallic she cannot name but cannot escape. Loud noises on the platform, a door slamming in the crew room, a sudden change in engine pressure - any of these can trigger the same collapse, flooding her with images she cannot sequence and a physical certainty that she is back there, small and useless. When her own heart begins to race - from exertion, from caffeine, from the ordinary stress of her job - she interprets the sensation as warning, as evidence that something terrible is imminent, and the memory surges forward again. The triggers and the memories have become nearly indistinguishable from one another.

The heightened threat she feels, particularly at night, feeds directly back into that same sensory loop. Valentina now checks the locks on her apartment door three or four times before bed, and she sleeps with a light on - though she has not told her supervisor that fatigue from disrupted sleep has begun to affect her concentration on early-morning runs. Any unexpected sound in the building sends her heart racing before she has consciously registered what she heard, and that somatic alarm reactivates the memories with fresh urgency, which in turn persuades her that the danger she perceives is real and present. She has come to believe, with a quiet and terrible certainty, that she cannot stop bad things from happening - that her helplessness as a child was not circumstantial but constitutional - and this conviction is reinforced each time the threat monitoring finds something to confirm it.

To manage all of this, Valentina has built a life structured around not stopping. She picks up extra shifts, volunteers for overnight runs, fills every gap with motion. But busyness, she has found, is not the same as safety: the quiet moments it was designed to prevent still arrive, and when they do, the memories return with the force of things that have been suppressed rather than processed. She has begun restricting her eating - skipping meals, sometimes going most of a day without food - in a way she describes vaguely as not having an appetite, though she also acknowledges it gives her a feeling of control she cannot locate elsewhere. She spends time imagining how different her life would have been if her father had never been violent, rehearsing alternative histories that leave her feeling more implicated in the real one, more certain that something she did or failed to do shaped what happened. These strategies have not quieted the memories; if anything, they have kept the triggers closer to the surface, so that the next loud noise or dark corridor finds her already primed.

What finally brought Valentina to seek help was a near-miss incident on the line three weeks ago: a loud bang from a mechanical fault caused her to freeze at the controls for several seconds, the past and present indistinguishable. She has not told her employer what happened. What she is most afraid of is that she will hurt someone through her own paralysis - that the child who watched and did nothing has become an adult who will do the same. What she is most hoping for, though she struggles to say it plainly, is to be convinced that she was not, and is not, the reason any of this happened.
